questions.q: Did God really order the killing of the Canaanites?
questions.h: Why did God command the destruction of the Canaanites
questions.t: This is the most serious moral objection raised against the Old Testament, and the honest starting point is what the texts actually say: the commands include women and children (Deuteronomy 20:16–18, 1 Samuel 15:3), and no Christian should pretend otherwise. Several things are true alongside that. The judgement falls on specific nations for specific practices, including child sacrifice, and Genesis 15:16 says it was delayed four hundred years until their sin reached its full measure. It is limited to one time and place and never given as a pattern for anyone since. God applied the same standard to Israel, sending them into exile for the same sins, and Rahab and her family were spared when she turned to him. Many scholars also argue that ancient war reports used deliberately sweeping language — 'left no survivors' — since the same peoples reappear shortly afterwards in the same books; others find that argument insufficient, and it does not by itself remove the commands. Christians have responded by seeing this as God's unique judicial act as judge of all the earth, by reading the conquest as a limited episode within a larger story, or by admitting they cannot fully reconcile it and holding it alongside the character of God shown at the cross. That last answer is more honest than a tidy one.

questions.q: Does the Bible approve of slavery?
questions.h: Does the Bible approve of slavery
questions.t: The honest answer is that the law regulated an institution that existed everywhere in the ancient world rather than abolishing it, as Jesus said of divorce, because of hardness of heart. The hardest texts must be faced first. Leviticus 25:44–46 permits buying foreign slaves as inheritable property for life, on different terms from Hebrew servants who went free after six years. Exodus 21:20–21 penalises a master who kills a slave outright but not one whose slave survives a day or two, adding the chilling reason that the slave is his property. Christians should not explain these away. Alongside them stand provisions unlike anything in surrounding law codes: kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (21:16), an injured slave went free (21:26–27), and a runaway was not to be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15). The New Testament never commands slavery and plants principles that undid it — every person made in God's image, no slave or free in Christ, Philemon receiving Onesimus as a brother — which Wilberforce and the abolitionists drew on directly. Christians have answered the remaining difficulty in different ways: that God accommodated law to a hard society while pointing beyond it, or that these regulations limited an evil he did not yet abolish. Neither answer makes the texts comfortable.

questions.q: Is hell real, and is it for ever?
questions.h: Is hell real, and eternal
questions.t: Jesus speaks about judgement more often than anyone else in the New Testament, and this verse sets eternal punishment directly beside eternal life, using the same word. The historic Christian view, held across Catholic, Orthodox and nearly all Protestant traditions, is that hell is real and final. A minority of evangelicals, including John Stott, who held the view tentatively, have argued that the lost are ultimately destroyed rather than punished for ever. Both views take judgement seriously. What Scripture is clear on is that judgement is just, that no one will be condemned unfairly, and that Jesus himself came so that no one has to face it.

questions.q: Why does God allow suffering?
questions.h: Does God cause suffering
questions.t: This verse is often quoted too quickly to people in pain. It does not say everything is good, or that suffering is not real. It says that God works in all things for the good of those who love him — and verse 29 defines that good as being made like Christ. Scripture never gives a full explanation for why particular suffering happens; Job is told a great deal about God and nothing about the reasons. What it gives is the cross, where God himself suffered, and the promise of verse 18 that present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come. If you are grieving, lament first; the explanation can wait.

questions.q: What do Christians believe about sexuality?
questions.h: What Christians believe about sexuality
questions.t: This is a subject men are regularly asked about, so it is worth being clear and kind at the same time. The historic teaching of the church, across every major tradition and still held by the great majority of Christians worldwide, is that sexual intimacy belongs within marriage between a man and a woman. Paul's point in this passage is that when people turn from God, desire becomes disordered — and he immediately goes on in chapter 2 to say that everyone who judges others is guilty too. Some recent scholars read these verses as addressing only exploitative practices of Paul's day; most evangelical and Reformed scholars have not found that persuasive. Whatever the question, no one is more sinful than anyone else, every person is made in God's image and deserves dignity, and 1 Corinthians 6:11 — 'such were some of you' — is the note the gospel always sounds.

questions.q: Why would God ask Abraham to sacrifice his son?
questions.h: Why would God ask Abraham to do this
questions.t: This is one of the hardest chapters in Scripture and it is right to find it disturbing. Three things help. First, the reader is told at the outset it is a test, and God stops it; child sacrifice is condemned elsewhere in the law as detestable, so the chapter is not endorsing it. Second, Abraham tells his servants that he and the boy will both come back, and Hebrews 11:19 says he reasoned God could raise the dead. Third, the substitute is provided on the very mountain where the temple would stand, and 'God will provide the lamb' is fulfilled when the Father does not spare his own Son. The chapter points beyond itself.

questions.q: Did God make Pharaoh sin?
questions.h: Did God make Pharaoh sin
questions.t: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it, and the sequence matters. God announces in advance, before any plague, that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21, 7:3); through the first five plagues the text describes Pharaoh hardening his own; from 9:12 it says the LORD hardened it. The historic Reformed reading is that God's announced purpose and Pharaoh's real choices are both true, and that God gave him over to a resistance he had already chosen — confirming a hard heart rather than corrupting a willing one. Others hold that God's hardening is judicial withdrawal, letting Pharaoh have his way. Paul takes up the episode in Romans 9 to show God's freedom in mercy, and answers the objection it raises rather than removing it. Scripture holds sovereignty and responsibility together without resolving the tension, and so should we.

questions.q: Can I know that I am really saved?
questions.h: Can I know I am saved
questions.t: John wrote this letter so that believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance does not rest on feelings, which come and go, but on three things John keeps returning to: believing that Jesus is the Son of God come in the flesh, a real if imperfect desire to obey him, and love for other Christians. The Reformed position is that those truly in Christ will persevere to the end because God keeps them. If you are anxious about whether you are really a Christian, that anxiety is itself worth bringing to someone who knows you.

questions.q: Why does God not answer some prayers?
questions.h: When prayer seems unanswered
questions.t: Jesus' promises about prayer are real and bold, but they sit inside the rest of Scripture, where Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and was not spared, and Paul's thorn was not removed. The historic Christian understanding is that God always hears and always answers in love, sometimes by giving what we ask, sometimes by giving something better, and sometimes by giving himself in the waiting. Unanswered prayer is not usually evidence of weak faith; it is one of the ordinary experiences of every believer in Scripture.

questions.q: What if someone prays for healing and it does not come?
questions.h: Prayer for the sick, and when healing does not come
questions.t: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the sick person. Christians read this in different ways: as a promise of healing now, as including ultimate resurrection, or as a general principle rather than a guarantee. What is clear is that failure to be healed is never presented in Scripture as proof that someone lacked faith — Paul left Trophimus sick, and his own thorn was not removed. Pray boldly, and never add guilt to someone's illness.

questions.q: Can a Christian pray the violent psalms?
questions.h: Can a Christian pray a psalm like this
questions.t: These verses are among the most shocking in the Bible. They are the honest cry of people who had watched their own children killed by Babylon, and the psalmist takes that rage to God instead of acting on it. The Psalms model bringing every emotion to God, including ones we should not act out. Christians read these psalms through the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies, and through God's promise that vengeance belongs to him. The appropriate response is not to pray the words against people we dislike, but to learn from them that God can bear the full weight of our anger and that justice is safe in his hands.

questions.q: Which Old Testament laws still apply to Christians?
questions.h: Which Old Testament laws still apply
questions.t: Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. The historic Reformed way of reading this distinguishes three kinds of law: the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still binds; the ceremonial law of sacrifices, food and cleanness, which is fulfilled in Christ and no longer practised (Hebrews and Acts 15); and the civil law of Israel as a nation, whose principles of justice remain instructive but which is not a code for modern states. Not every Christian tradition uses these categories, but the conclusion is widely shared.

questions.q: Why were Ananias and Sapphira struck down?
questions.h: Why did Ananias and Sapphira die
questions.t: Their sin was not keeping money back — Peter says it was theirs — but lying to God to appear more generous than they were, at the very foundation of the church. Luke records the fear it produced without softening it. The episode is exceptional rather than a pattern: the New Testament does not expect such judgement to follow every sin, and later passages show great patience with serious failure. It stands as a warning that God is not mocked, especially where religion becomes performance.

questions.q: How should I read the six days of creation?
questions.h: How Christians read the six days
questions.t: What this chapter teaches is not in dispute among Christians: God created everything out of nothing, deliberately, in order, and called it good, with humanity made last and in his image. How long it took is disputed, and honestly so. Some read the days as ordinary days; some as long ages; some as a literary framework arranging the acts of creation rather than timing them. All three are held by people who take Scripture as God's word. We would not make any of them a test of fellowship, and we would be cautious of anyone who does.

questions.q: Was Adam a real man?
questions.h: Was Adam a real man
questions.t: We hold that he was, and that this is not a side issue. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 sets one man's disobedience against one man's obedience, and it is hard to see how the comparison works if only one of the two ever existed. Some evangelical scholars now read Adam as representative rather than as the first individual; we think that costs more than it saves.

questions.q: Who should be baptised, and how?
questions.h: What baptism means, and what Christians dispute
questions.t: All agree it marks union with Christ in his death and resurrection. Two things are argued: who should be baptised, and how. Baptist churches baptise those who profess faith, by immersion; Presbyterian, Anglican and Reformed paedobaptist churches also baptise the children of believers, usually by pouring. Both appeal to covenant and to apostolic practice. It is a real difference and not a trivial one, but it has never been a boundary of the faith itself.

questions.q: What happens at the Lord's Supper?
questions.h: What happens at the table
questions.t: Christians have divided over this for five hundred years. Roman Catholics hold the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; Lutherans that he is present in and with them; the Reformed that he is truly present to faith by the Spirit though the elements do not change; and many evangelicals that it is chiefly a memorial. We stand with the Reformed view, and we would not refuse the table to a brother holding any of the others. What nobody disputes is that Jesus commanded it and that it proclaims his death until he comes.

questions.q: Does God choose who is saved?
questions.h: The chapter Christians argue over most
questions.t: We take Paul to be teaching that God's choice of individuals rests on his mercy rather than on anything foreseen in them, which is the Reformed reading and the one this group holds; the Westminster Confession 3.5 states it directly, that God chose his people without any foresight of faith or works in them. Others read the chapter as concerning nations and roles in redemptive history rather than eternal destinies, or as election based on foreseen faith. Paul anticipates the objection in verse 19 and does not soften it, which is itself worth weighing. Hold the doctrine the way Paul does here — alongside the grief of verses 1 to 3.

questions.q: Are the spiritual gifts still given today?
questions.h: Are these gifts for today
questions.t: This is a live disagreement among evangelicals and within Reformed churches. Cessationists hold that the revelatory and sign gifts ceased with the apostles; continuationists that the Spirit still gives them, while insisting everything be tested by Scripture. Both are held by serious people. What Paul actually argues in this chapter is not about timing at all: the gifts differ, the Spirit does not, and they exist for the common good rather than for display.

questions.q: What does the Bible say about men and women in the church?
questions.h: Men and women in the church
questions.t: This passage is the centre of a long and honest disagreement among evangelicals. Complementarians read it as restricting the teaching and governing office of the church to qualified men, on the basis of the creation order Paul cites. Egalitarians read it as addressing a specific disorder in Ephesus. Reformed churches are overwhelmingly complementarian and that is where this group stands; we also recognise that the other position is held by people who love Scripture. Note what the passage does not say: nothing here concerns a woman's worth, ability or standing before God.

questions.q: What is the thousand years in Revelation?
questions.h: How to hold a passage like this
questions.t: Christians who agree on everything else divide over the thousand years, and have since the early centuries. Amillennialists read it as the present age between the cross and the return; postmillennialists as a coming era of gospel success; premillennialists as a literal reign after Christ returns. Each can point to real evidence. What all three hold is what the chapter is actually for: Christ reigns, his people are secure, and evil is finally and completely dealt with.

questions.q: Who did Christ die for?
questions.h: For whose sins
questions.t: John says Christ is the atoning sacrifice for our sins and also for the sins of the whole world. Reformed Christians have read that as the cross being sufficient for all and effective for those who believe; others read it as an atonement made equally for everyone and applied on condition of faith. The difference is real and it has never stopped either side preaching Christ freely to anyone who will listen. Note the pastoral setting: John raises it to comfort people who have sinned, not to settle a debate.

questions.q: What did Jesus teach about divorce and remarriage?
questions.h: Divorce and remarriage
questions.t: Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality, and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Beyond those two, Christians differ over whether remarriage is permitted, and churches take genuinely different positions. This is a place to seek counsel from your own church rather than settle it from a note. What is not in doubt is that Jesus treats marriage as a lifelong covenant instituted at creation, and that he says so to people looking for a loophole.

questions.q: Can a true Christian fall away?
questions.h: Better things in your case
questions.t: Read the warning of verses 4 to 8 with this verse attached, because the writer attaches it himself. Our position is the historic Reformed one, set out in the Westminster Confession 17.1: those whom God has accepted can neither totally nor finally fall away, and the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep them. The Remonstrant tradition, following Arminius, holds the opposite. Others read the passage as describing believers who can genuinely be lost. Either way the warning is meant to be felt rather than explained away.

questions.q: Is there still a future for Israel?
questions.h: Is there a future for Israel
questions.t: Paul says a hardening has come on Israel in part, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and then all Israel will be saved. What that means is debated: a large-scale future turning of Jewish people to Christ, or the sum of elect Jews and Gentiles across history, or the church as the true Israel. The first has been the most common reading in the Reformed tradition and is probably the most natural here. The text does not settle it as tightly as either side usually claims.

Anxiety and worry.g: Anxiety is answered by knowing the Father who provides, and by seeking his kingdom first.
Fear of God displaces fear of people, because the Father's care reaches the smallest detail.
Fear of God displaces fear of people, and the Father's care reaches the smallest detail.
Anxiety is answered by the Father's pleasure in giving his children the kingdom.

Money and possessions.g: Religion performed for an audience has already received all the reward it will get.
What you treasure shapes what you love.

Money and possessions.h: The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl
Money and possessions.g: The kingdom is worth everything, and those who see it give up all they have with joy.
Entry into the kingdom is humanly impossible and possible only as God's gift.

Money and possessions.h: The Parable of the Rich Fool
Money and possessions.g: A life built on accumulation ends with everything going to someone else.
Giving away what cannot be kept secures what cannot be lost.
How wealth is used in this life has consequences in the next, and Scripture is sufficient warning.
God's power is displayed through human weakness, and present suffering prepares an eternal glory.
Christian giving flows from the grace of Christ, who became poor to make us rich.
Contentment comes from Christ's strength, not from circumstances.

Marriage.g: Purity is a matter of the heart, and sin must be dealt with decisively.
Jesus treats marriage as binding, against a culture of easy divorce.
Jesus grounds marriage in God's creation design rather than in the law's concessions.
Jesus refuses both condemnation and approval: he forgives and calls to a new life.
Marriage is good and mutual, and should be preserved wherever possible.
Christian marriage is meant to picture the relationship between Christ and his church.
Christian marriage is marked by respect and honour on both sides, and can itself be a witness.
History's goal is a wedding: Christ united with his people.

Suffering and persecution.g: Jesus forewarns his followers so that persecution will not shake their faith.
Paul's credentials as an apostle are his sufferings for Christ, not his achievements.
Paul measures his circumstances by what they do for the gospel, not what they do for him.
The heart of the gospel mystery is Christ living in his people and their future glory with him.
Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel, because God, who saved by his own grace, gives power to endure.
Trials, rightly received, are God's means of growing mature faith.
Believers endure suffering patiently because the Lord is coming and is merciful.
Christ's suffering is both the pattern for believers to follow and the sacrifice that bore their sins.
Believers can answer for their hope with gentleness because Christ suffered once to bring them to God.
Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong, but a share in his sufferings.

Prayer.g: Prayer begins with God's name, kingdom and will, and only then turns to our needs.
Jesus touches the untouchable, and cleanness passes from him to the man.
Jesus' human will genuinely recoils and genuinely submits to the Father.
Jesus is directed by his mission and his communion with the Father, not by the demands of the crowd.
Jesus' holiness is not endangered by contact with the unclean; instead it overcomes the uncleanness.
In his hour of greatest distress Jesus submits his own will to the Father's.
The Son alone reveals the Father, and does so to the childlike rather than the clever.
Jesus teaches his disciples to address God simply as Father.
Eternal life consists in knowing the Father and the Son, and Jesus shared the Father's glory before creation.
Jesus prays that his people be kept, united and made holy by God's word as they are sent into the world.

Temptation and sin.g: Where Israel failed under testing, Jesus succeeds, and does so by Scripture.
Causing another believer to fall is among the gravest sins Jesus names.
Correction begins privately and aims at winning the brother, not exposing him.

Temptation and sin.h: The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus
Temptation and sin.g: Jesus arrives announcing that God's long-promised rule is now breaking in.
Sin is to be dealt with drastically, because the stakes are final.
Jesus resists by Scripture what Israel failed, and the conflict is only postponed.
Jesus refuses to treat suffering as proof of particular guilt, and turns the question into a call to repent.
Correction and ready forgiveness belong together in the church.
Bringing back a brother who has wandered is among the most important things a believer can do.

The cross and atonement.g: Following Jesus means the cross, and the only life worth keeping is the one given away.
The mockers speak more truly than they know: to save others, he would not save himself.
The way of the Messiah through the cross becomes the way for everyone who follows him.
Following Jesus means a daily cross, and only the life given away is kept.
From the cross Jesus forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying criminal.
Even at the cross, Scripture is fulfilled and Jesus cares for those he loves.
God's love was shown to his enemies, which is why believers can be certain of final salvation.
In response to God's mercy, believers offer their whole lives as worship and serve one another with their different gifts.
The cross looks like weakness and foolishness, but it is God's power and wisdom for salvation.
Christ took the law's curse upon himself so that its blessing could reach those who believe.

The resurrection.g: Jesus proves the resurrection from the very books his opponents accepted.
Jesus' enemies remember his prediction better than his disciples do.
The tomb is empty, and the risen Jesus is worshipped by the first witnesses.
Jesus affirms the resurrection from the very Scriptures his opponents claimed to rely on.
The crucified Jesus has risen, and even Peter, who denied him, is named in the invitation to meet him.
Jesus proves the resurrection from the books his opponents accepted.
The first witnesses to the resurrection are women whose testimony the apostles dismiss.
The empty tomb and the grave cloths left behind point to resurrection, not theft.
The gospel rests on historical events: Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection and appearances to many witnesses.
Christianity stands or falls on the historical resurrection of Jesus.

The Holy Spirit.g: Jesus promises the Spirit as another Helper like himself, who will live in his people and teach them.

The Holy Spirit.h: The Promise of the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit.g: The Spirit's work is to convict the world and to glorify Christ by making him known.
The Spirit comes on all God's people, and the gospel is heard immediately in every language.

The Holy Spirit.h: The Gentiles Receive the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit.g: God gives Gentiles the same Spirit, settling the question before the church can debate it.

The Holy Spirit.h: The Holy Spirit Received at Ephesus
The Holy Spirit.g: Followers of John's preparatory message are brought into the full Christian gospel.
Because Christ bore condemnation, those in him face none, and the Spirit gives them new life.

The Holy Spirit.h: Paul's Message by the Spirit's Power
The Holy Spirit.g: Faith that rests on God's power, not on persuasive technique, is the kind that lasts.

The Holy Spirit.h: The Temple of the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit.g: The body matters to God, is the Spirit's temple, and belongs to Christ who bought it.
The Spirit produces in believers the character the law demanded but could not create.
Teaching must be tested by what it says about Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.

The church.g: Persecution scatters the church, which fulfils Jesus' command to go to Judea and Samaria.
A church of Jews and Gentiles together becomes the springboard for the mission to the world.
Loyalty to human leaders divides the church, which belongs to Christ alone.
Every believer is a necessary part of Christ's body, and all share one another's sufferings and joys.
The cross reconciles people to God and, in the same act, to each other.
Unity in the church depends on humility that puts others first.
The heart of the gospel mystery is Christ living in his people and their future glory with him.
The risen Christ, who freed his people by his blood, is coming visibly as ruler of all earthly kings.
Sound doctrine and hard work are not enough if love has been lost.
Christ does not promise to spare his suffering people, but to keep them through death into life.

The Lord's Supper and baptism.g: Jesus identifies himself with the people he came to save, and the Father and Spirit confirm who he is.
Jesus interprets his own death in advance as the covenant sacrifice for the forgiveness of sins.
Jesus explains his death in advance as a covenant sacrifice, and gives his followers a meal by which to remember it.
Luke alone notes that Jesus was praying — one of many such notes in this Gospel.
Jesus gives his coming death the meaning of a new covenant, and commands the meal as remembrance.
The Lord's Supper proclaims Christ's death and must be shared in a way that honours all his people.

Evangelism and mission.g: The messengers travel light and depend on hospitality, carrying the kingdom's authority.
Endurance under pressure marks genuine faith, and the gospel will reach all nations first.
The risen Christ sends his people to all nations with all authority and his abiding presence.
Jesus is directed by his mission and his communion with the Father, not by the demands of the crowd.
Jesus' mission now extends through those he has called and sent.
Jesus refuses to let popularity in one place limit his mission.
The mission extends through those Jesus has called and equipped.
Persecution becomes an opportunity to bear witness, and Christ himself supplies the words.
Becoming a child of God comes by receiving Christ, and is God's doing rather than human descent or decision.

Leadership.g: Jesus is the promised shepherd, who gives his life freely for his sheep.
Church leaders must be men of proven character, able to teach, whose homes show how they would care for God's church.
Those who serve the church practically must share the same godly character as its leaders.
Faithful elders should be supported and protected from false accusation, and held accountable when they sin.
Church leaders are chosen above all for proven character and faithfulness to sound teaching.
Church leaders are under-shepherds who serve willingly and lead by example, answerable to Christ.

Humility and pride.g: Greatness in the kingdom means the lowliness of a child.
The debt God has forgiven is beyond calculation, which makes refusing to forgive unthinkable.
Greatness in Jesus' kingdom is measured by service to the least, not by rank.
Greatness is receiving the insignificant, and Jesus' work is wider than his disciples' circle.
At the table where he gives himself, Jesus redefines greatness as service.

Humility and pride.h: Christ the Servant of Jews and Gentiles
Humility and pride.g: Christ welcomed Jews and Gentiles alike, so his people must welcome one another.
Christian leaders answer to the Lord, and the apostles' suffering exposes the Corinthians' pride.
Paul adapts everything except the gospel itself in order to reach people.

Love for others.g: God's children are to reflect his indiscriminate kindness, even toward enemies.
God's children are to imitate his kindness toward those who do not deserve it.
The mark of Jesus' disciples is love for one another, measured by his love for them.
Genuine love shows itself in honour, zeal, patience, prayer and hospitality among believers.
The freedom of the gospel is lived out in gentle restoration, shared burdens and persistent good.
Brotherly love shows itself in hospitality, care for sufferers and faithfulness in marriage.
Love is defined by Christ's self-giving and proved by practical help to those in need.
Supporting those who carry the gospel makes believers partners in their work.

Speech and the tongue.g: Gifts used in the gathered church must build up others and be understandable.
Believers are to pray for gospel opportunities and speak graciously to those outside the church.
The tongue reveals and shapes the whole person, and cannot be controlled without God's help.
All plans should be made in humble dependence on God's will, since life is brief.

Judgement and the end.h: The Return of the Son of Man
Judgement and the end.g: Christ's return will be unmistakable and universal, needing no announcement.

Judgement and the end.h: The Return of the Son of Man
Judgement and the end.g: However the sequence is understood, the story ends with the Son of Man coming in power to gather his people.

Judgement and the end.h: The Return of the Son of Man
Judgement and the end.g: For God's people, the signs that terrify the world are grounds to lift their heads.
Those who condemn others while doing the same things are equally under God's judgement.
Believers do not know when Christ will come, so they live ready, as people of the day.
The God who created and once judged the world will certainly judge it again.
The apparent delay in Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance.
The faith has been delivered once for all, and must be defended against those who twist grace into licence.
God's final judgements proceed from his own holiness.

Judgement and the end.h: Judgment before the Great White Throne
Judgement and the end.g: Everyone will stand before God, and judgement will be according to a full and accurate record.

Doubt and unbelief.h: The Unbelief of the Jewish Leaders
Doubt and unbelief.g: Those sent to arrest Jesus are arrested by his words instead.
Unbelief in the face of clear signs is both human refusal and, as Isaiah foretold, divine hardening.
Israel stumbled by seeking righteousness through works instead of receiving it by faith.
Believers guard one another against hardening by daily encouragement.

False teaching.g: Believers must guard the church's unity against divisive teachers, trusting God's victory over evil.
False teachers can look impressive and spiritual; the test is whether they preach the true Jesus.
Adding anything to Christ as a condition of salvation does not improve the gospel; it replaces it.
Sound teaching aims at love, not speculation.
False teaching is exposed by the way its teachers live.
Pointless disputes damage the church, and persistently divisive people must be firmly dealt with.
God will judge false teachers who exploit the church, and will rescue those who belong to him.
Denying the Son means denying the Father, whatever religious claims are made.
Love for the truth means refusing to support those who deny Christ's coming in the flesh.

The poor and the vulnerable.g: Religion performed for an audience has already received all the reward it will get.
True devotion is measured by cost, not amount — even as the institution receiving it faces judgement.
Jesus raises the dead out of compassion for a woman nobody else could help.

The poor and the vulnerable.h: The Parable of the Persistent Widow
The poor and the vulnerable.g: God is not like the unjust judge, so his people should keep praying and not give up.
God measures giving by what is kept back, not by the amount given.
Families must care for their own, and the church for those who have no one else.
